summary:
Across 13 evals (24 iterations), results consistently favor with_skill on expected-output match and assertion pass rates, but without_skill is faster and cheaper everywhere a comparison exists, and the few direct quality-judgment comparisons that were run are mixed or favor without_skill.

Expected output and assertions:
- In every eval where both variants have data, with_skill met the expected output as often or more often than without_skill (e.g. no-guardrail-on-production-path, draft-not-pinned-trap, blocked-sometimes-no-account, invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection, bpa-dormant-keys, gr-no-apply all show with_skill at 100% expected-output match vs. without_skill at 0% or lower assertion scores). The one exception is api-key-inventory, where both variants failed the expected-output check (0/1) despite with_skill passing far more individual assertions (9/11 vs 2/11) — the overall expected-output bar is strict and neither variant cleared it there.
- Three evals (version-limit-counts-draft, pii-entry-with-only-action, gr-prompt-attack) have no without_skill data at all (marked null), so no direct comparison is possible there; with_skill alone passed 100% of assertions in each.
- Several assertions pass for both variants regardless of eval (e.g. "does not claim to have modified any resource," "discloses which paths/regions were not covered," "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" in most cases) — these are not differentiating.
- Some assertions fail for both variants consistently (e.g. the "expired vs inactive key" distinction in api-key-inventory, the "strong DRAFT says nothing about older pinned version" point in draft-not-pinned-trap, the "staged deactivate-before-delete" sequencing in bpa-dormant-keys, and the "GRD catalog check-id" presence in gr-no-apply) — these point to shared gaps in behavior or possibly in how the assertion itself is written, not a variant-specific weakness.
- A few assertions split cleanly, with with_skill passing and without_skill failing (docs link citation and no-12-digit-number checks in api-key-inventory; several specificity/read-only framing checks in no-guardrail-on-production-path and invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection). No assertions in this dataset show without_skill passing while with_skill fails.

Runtime and cost:
- without_skill is consistently and often substantially faster and cheaper than with_skill across every eval with paired metrics (e.g. 22s/$0.19 vs 3m23s/$1.69 on no-guardrail-on-production-path; 12s/$0.10 vs 14s/$0.12 on blocked-sometimes-no-account as the smallest gap; 52s/$0.44 vs 1m29s/$0.75 on bpa-dormant-keys). with_skill also shows higher context-window utilization throughout, consistent with longer/more thorough runs.

Direct quality judgments (pairwise LLM comparison):
- Only two evals produced any quality comparison pairs (bpa-dormant-keys and gr-no-apply); all other evals had this comparison skipped (not applicable or no pair to compare), so quality-judgment coverage is very sparse.
- In bpa-dormant-keys, the one evaluated pair favored without_skill on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), at medium confidence — this runs counter to the assertion-level pattern favoring with_skill in that same eval, where with_skill still had a higher assertion pass rate (4/5 vs 2/5) and matched the expected output while without_skill also matched but with lower assertion coverage.
- In gr-no-apply, the one pair was split evenly (2 favored each, 2 comparable) across criteria, at medium confidence — essentially a tie.
- Given only two pairs total and medium confidence, this quality dimension is a weak, low-coverage signal and shouldn't be weighted heavily against the stronger, broader assertion-level and expected-output patterns.

Other notes:
- Two evals (scp-impact-before-applying, and the two "should_trigger: false" evals throttling-question-does-not-trigger and neg-invoke-access-denied) were skipped for expected-output/assertions/quality comparisons, either because they don't apply or because the trigger wasn't expected to fire; these are absent data, not failures for either variant.
- Output consistency across repeated runs could not be assessed for any eval (all null), so run-to-run stability is unknown for both variants.
- Confidence levels on expected-output judgments are mostly "high," giving reasonable reliability to the expected-output/assertion findings, though a few individual assertions (e.g. the expired/inactive key distinction, draft-strength wording) carry "low" or "medium" confidence and should be read cautiously.

Overall, this is a tradeoff pattern: with_skill tends to meet expected outputs and pass assertions more often across most evals with paired data, while without_skill is markedly faster and cheaper and, in the very limited direct quality-judgment comparisons available, performed as well as or better than with_skill. No single dimension provides a conclusive verdict, and three evals had no without_skill data at all, limiting the overall comparison's completeness.

Note: a DevOps Agent endpoint outage failed some runs in this pass. Those scenarios (gr-prompt-attack, pii-entry-with-only-action, scp-impact-before-applying, version-limit-counts-draft) were rerun on the same agent spaces with the same settings, and their results replace the failed runs.

This evaluation covers a single chat task about auditing Amazon Bedrock API keys. The trigger behavior under test did fire (1/1).

Expected output: Both variants failed to meet the overall expected output (0/1 for each), so on this top-level measure neither variant succeeded. Confidence in this judgment was high for without_skill and medium for with_skill, so this is a reasonably solid (not low-confidence) finding of failure for both.

Assertions (11 total, finer-grained): with_skill passed 9/11 (82%), without_skill passed 2/11 (18%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions passed for both variants ("never prints a full API key ID/alias/username" and "no full access key ID or Bedrock key ID exposed with sensitive prefix") — these are not differentiating; both variants handle key-masking/redaction correctly.
- One assertion failed for both variants ("states grant/risk tier and removal steps per key") — this indicates a capability gap or an assertion criterion neither variant satisfies, worth noting as a shared weakness rather than a difference between variants.
- One assertion ("expired vs inactive key re-enablement treatment") failed for both variants, and notably with_skill's failure here was rated low confidence, meaning that specific measurement is weak evidence.
- The remaining seven assertions all follow a "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern, covering things like listing all account-wide API keys, correctly stating IAM's lack of last-used reporting, confirming read-only/no-change behavior, not ending with a follow-up question, citing AWS docs, and avoiding exposure of account numbers. These passes/fails were rated at medium-to-high confidence, so this is a fairly consistent and credible difference in favor of with_skill on many specific behavioral checks, even though the overall expected-output judgment still marked with_skill as failing.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (23s vs 1m1s) and cheaper ($0.19 vs $0.51), with lower context-window utilization (4.4% vs 13.4%). This is a clear efficiency difference favoring without_skill, but it comes alongside without_skill failing many more of the detailed assertions, so it represents a speed/cost-vs-thoroughness tradeoff rather than a strict advantage.

Quality comparison: No comparable quality pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal to report here.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this evaluation.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-run evaluation, so confidence in generalizing is limited. Within this one task, with_skill satisfied more of the specific assertion-level criteria (especially around completeness of key listing, correct caveats about IAM's lack of last-used data, read-only framing, and documentation citation) while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper and used less context. Neither variant satisfied the overall expected-output criterion or the assertion about stating per-key risk tier and removal guidance, pointing to a shared gap. One assertion difference (re-enablement treatment) rests on a low-confidence judgment for with_skill and should be treated cautiously.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, high confidence). Per-assertion results: with_skill passed all 8 assertions (8/8, 100%), while without_skill passed only 1 of 8 (12%). Of the 8 assertions:
- 7 assertions followed the same pattern: with_skill passed and without_skill failed. These cover a range of substantive requirements — correctly identifying affected users by name, clarifying that IAM roles/Identity Center users are unaffected, framing the SCP as a draft template rather than something applied, disclosing audit scope limitations, avoiding a trailing follow-up question, citing AWS documentation, and avoiding exposure of 12-digit account numbers.
- 1 assertion ("no exposed access key ID") passed for both variants — this one doesn't differentiate them, since neither variant exposed key material.
Most of these failing assertions carry high or medium confidence from the LLM evaluator, so the pattern of without_skill underperforming appears to be a reasonably reliable finding rather than a measurement artifact.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was notably faster (1m0s vs 2m16s) and cheaper ($0.50 vs $1.13) than with_skill. Context window utilization was low for both (5.3% vs 7.7%), with no compaction needed in either case. So without_skill is the leaner, lower-cost run, but it is paired here with substantially lower correctness on the content requirements being tested.

Quality comparison and consistency: No quality pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), and output-consistency data is null for both variants, so there is no information on run-to-run stability or a separate quality-preference judgment to weigh in. These dimensions are simply absent data, not a negative signal for either variant.

Overall picture: This eval presents a tradeoff in resource usage (without_skill cheaper and faster) set against a substantial difference in meeting the expected output and passing content assertions (with_skill passing nearly all checks, without_skill passing almost none). Since the task-correctness measurements are based on a single run each with mostly high-confidence judgments, the finding is suggestive but rests on an n=1 comparison rather than repeated-trial evidence, and broader quality/consistency metrics that could add additional context were not available here.

Expected output: both variants were judged to meet the expected output in their one trial (1/1, 100%). Confidence in that judgment was high for with_skill and only medium for without_skill, so without_skill's "pass" should be read with somewhat less certainty.

- Two assertions passed for both variants ("reports last-used evidence rather than asserting dormancy" and "distinguishes dormant from safe to remove") — these did not differentiate the variants.

- Two assertions split: with_skill passed and without_skill failed on "does not write full key identifiers" (high confidence) and on "no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed" (regex-based, deterministic). These are notable because they involve exposure of sensitive identifying information, and without_skill failed both in this single run.

Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 4/5 (80%), without_skill 2/5 (40%), driven mainly by the two information-exposure assertions above.

Quality comparison (LLM-judged, one pair evaluated): favored without_skill on all 4 scored aspects (accuracy x2, actionability, completeness), with medium average confidence. This is based on a single comparison pair, so it reflects one instance rather than a broad pattern, and sits in tension with the assertion results, which favored with_skill on the exposure-related checks.

One run (likely with_skill's) exceeded the 30-second runtime threshold used for comparison.

Output consistency: not available for either variant (no data recorded), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the picture is mixed and based on a very small sample (one task, one run each), so all findings should be treated as preliminary. Variant_a passed more assertions, notably two tied to avoiding exposure of sensitive identifiers (full key IDs and raw account IDs), while without_skill was favored in the separate LLM quality comparison on accuracy, actionability, and completeness, and was faster and cheaper to run. Both variants shared a common failure on the staged deactivate-before-delete assertion, pointing to a possible shared gap rather than a difference between them.
